about: CMB-064: claims-probe hits read against their registry rows and kept, with the reason. claims_probe.py marks them [read] and counts them apart. An entry matches one exact sentence on one page; when the sentence changes, the entry goes stale and the probe says so: read it again, then update or drop the entry. Add an entry only after reading the sentence against the row it names.

entries.sentence: The evidence behind each risk is in BMI and health risks ; for a BMI under 18.5, see underweight BMI risks .

entries.sentence: Muscle mass tends to fall with age, so the same BMI can mean more body fat; the American Diabetes Association notes that this may lead to obesity being missed in older adults.
entries.why: the ADA Standards' line, named in the sentence: loss of muscle mass in older adults "may lead to underdiagnosis of obesity" (ada-2026-obesity-standards)

entries.sentence: BMI is CDC’s formula (US units × 703, or kg/m²), shown to 0.1.
entries.why: "shown to" is the display precision, not a study claim; the formula is CDC's (cdc-calculating-bmi)

entries.sentence: Clinicians still use IBW equations “to calculate drug dosing, to estimate overweight and underweight statuses, and to calculate nutrient intakes,” Peterson and colleagues write.
entries.why: a quote the sentence attributes to Peterson and colleagues (peterson-2016-ibw)

entries.sentence: Peterson and colleagues write that it “was originally defined as the weight associated with the greatest life expectancy at each height” and that “IBW equations are still being used by clinicians to calculate drug dosing, to estimate overweight and underweight statuses, and to calculate nutrient intakes.”
entries.why: quotes the sentence attributes to Peterson and colleagues (peterson-2016-ibw)

entries.sentence: Pai and Paloucek concluded that “any one of these equations may be used to estimate IBW.” Robinson and colleagues found that estimates “obtained by the widely used empirical method probably contain only minor errors.” Peterson and colleagues point out that the equations give a single weight, where most clinicians favor a range.
entries.why: quotes the sentences attribute to Pai and Paloucek, Robinson and colleagues, and Peterson and colleagues (pai-paloucek-2000-ibw, robinson-1983-ibw, peterson-2016-ibw)

entries.sentence: Trefethen says his formula is “not based on epidemiological studies” and may not be an improvement.

entries.sentence: “I am an applied mathematician, not a doctor or an epidemiologist,” he writes, and the new formulas are “not based on epidemiological studies” and may not be an improvement.

entries.why: Trefethen's own words and his pointer to Heymsfield et al. 2007 (trefethen-new-bmi)

entries.sentence: Crude analyses that ignored smoking and existing disease gave exaggerated risks for underweight and inverted ones for overweight, so overweight looked protective.
entries.why: GBMC 2016, linked in the paragraph before; worded as the paper puts it (gbmc-2016-bmi-mortality, CMB-064 note)

entries.sentence: The authors could reproduce a 2013 review’s finding that overweight carried a lower risk of death in analyses with inadequate control for these biases, but not in the strict one.
entries.why: GBMC 2016, linked in the paragraph before; worded as the paper puts it (gbmc-2016-bmi-mortality, CMB-064 note)

entries.sentence: Hazard ratio for death by BMI band among 3,951,455 never-smokers without chronic disease; 1.20 means a 20% higher risk than at 22.5 to 24.9.
entries.why: the chart caption: GBMC 2016's hazard ratios and sample (gbmc-2016-bmi-mortality)

entries.sentence: Per 5 BMI units above 25, the risk of death in never-smokers was 39% higher in Europe and in East Asia, 31% in Australia and New Zealand and 29% in North America; the authors write that “the associations of both overweight and obesity with higher all-cause mortality were broadly consistent in four continents”.
entries.why: GBMC 2016's regional hazard ratios (1.39, 1.31, 1.29) and its own interpretation, quoted (gbmc-2016-bmi-mortality)
